key_insight: Language models should not be relied on to autonomously attribute or situate knowledge: they frequently fail to provide reliable provenance, context, and credibility judgments, so attribution needs dedicated systems, metadata and human oversight.
problem_solved: Addresses the challenge of misplaced trust in LLM-produced citations and contextual claims—highlighting risks of misattribution, decontextualized knowledge, and related epistemic and legal harms when attribution is left solely to the model.
method: Diagnose failure modes by analyzing examples where LLMs produce incorrect, incomplete, or unverifiable attributions and context.
Develop a conceptual framework that separates knowledge production from attribution and situating, emphasizing provenance, structured metadata, retrieval augmentation, and human-in-the-loop checks.
Offer practical recommendations and evaluation criteria for systems and policies that ensure accountable attribution (technical and governance measures).
impact: Signals a shift from trusting LLM outputs to engineering end-to-end attribution pipelines—practitioners must combine retrieval, provenance recording, transparency metrics and human review to build trustworthy systems and meet regulatory/ethical expectations.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: source documents → retrieval module → LM (content generation) → provenance recorder → human audit
Side-by-side examples: LLM output with incorrect/no citation vs. corrected output with verified provenance
Risk matrix chart: types of attribution failures (fabrication, miscontextualization, omission) vs. impact severity
Icon set: citation/book, magnifying glass (verification), shield (governance), hand (human oversight)
paper_title: Attributing and situating knowledge cannot be left to language models
